title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.6 Maps with Luxembourg examples
For a lightweight first map, we use polygon data from map_data("world") and zoom into Luxembourg.

world_map <- map_data("world")

ggplot(world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "grey90", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(4.5, 7.0), ylim = c(49.2, 50.4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg in regional context",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









world_map <- map_data("world")
communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

lux_map <- world_map |>
  filter(region == "Luxembourg")

# Step 1: regional background
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey92", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Step 1: Regional background",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
print(p1)

# Step 2: add commune polygons
p2 <- p1 +
  # Layer 2: commune polygons inside Luxembourg
  geom_polygon(
    data = communes_df,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "#fdebd0", color = "#d35400", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 2: + Commune polygons")
print(p2)

# Step 3: add Luxembourg country outline
p3 <- p2 +
  # Layer 3: Luxembourg country outline
  geom_polygon(
    data = lux_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 3: + Country outline")
print(p3)

# Step 4: add centroid points for important places
p4 <- p3 +
  # Layer 4: important city points from centroid file
  geom_point(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat),
    color = "navy", size = 1.8
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 4: + Important place points")
print(p4)

# Step 5: add city labels (final map)
p5 <- p4 +
  # Layer 5: city labels
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    size = 2.8, nudge_y = 0.015, color = "navy"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Step 5: Final map",
    subtitle = "Communes (polygons) + centroid city labels",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  )
print(p5)




































You can also combine the five map states into one overview grid:

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, ncol = 5)








Step-by-step map logic:

Load base map polygons (map_data("world")) and zoom to Luxembourg.
Add commune polygons from communes_df.RDS as an internal administrative layer.
Draw Luxembourg border on top for a clear country outline.
Add centroid points from centroids_label.RDS.
Add text labels for important places (label column).

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.7 Population per commune (choropleth)
This map visualizes total population (total_population) by commune.
How it works:

Load commune population table from Gemengen_Statistiken.qs.
Join population values to commune polygons via commune name (id vs COMMUNE_NOM).
Use fill = total_population to encode population with a color gradient.
Optionally add commune labels at centroids for orientation.


communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

# Preferred source: Gemengen_Statistiken.qs
pop_totals <- readRDS("Gemengen_Statistiken.RDS")

# Join population table to polygon coordinates
communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(
    pop_totals |>
      select(Gemeng, total_population = Awunnerzuel),
    by = c("id" = "Gemeng")
  )

Warning in left_join(communes_df, select(pop_totals, Gemeng, total_population = Awunnerzuel), : Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.

ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = total_population)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: total population by commune",
    subtitle = "Fill color = total_population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Interpretation:

Darker communes have lower population totals.
Luxembourg City should stand out clearly as the most populous commune.

2 What Cursor can help with

Drafting code templates (imports, joins, pipelines, plots).
Explaining existing code and suggesting refactors.
Debugging error messages and proposing fixes.
Generating short documentation snippets and comments.
Helping structure Quarto reports.

title: Session 5 — Using AI (Cursor) as coding assistant
text:
3 Prompt patterns for this course
Use prompts that include:

Context: what your data looks like and what packages you use.
Task: exact output you need (table, plot, function, interpretation).
Constraints: keep tidyverse style, avoid changing variable names, keep reproducibility.
Verification: ask for checks and edge cases.

Example prompt:

I have a tibble with variables speaker, genre, and token_count.
Write tidyverse code to compute median token count by genre and create a ggplot boxplot by genre.
Keep original variable names and add a short interpretation paragraph.

title: Session 5 — Using AI (Cursor) as coding assistant
text:
4 Human-in-the-loop workflow

Ask Cursor for a first draft.
Review every line of generated code.
Run code chunk by chunk.
Check whether output matches the research question.
Revise prompt and code until result is correct.
Document what was generated and what you changed manually.

title: Session 5 — Using AI (Cursor) as coding assistant
text:
5 Common failure modes

Fabricated column names or package functions.
Incorrect assumptions about data types or missing values.
Code that runs but does not answer your question.
Overly complex solutions for simple tasks.
Missing citations or weak methodological transparency.

title: Session 5 — Using AI (Cursor) as coding assistant
text:
6 Good practice and transparency

Keep AI support visible in your workflow notes.
Save intermediate steps and interpretation text in Quarto.
Prefer small, testable prompts over one large prompt.
Cross-check key results with simple summaries.

Session 4
text:
This map visualizes total population (total_population) by commune.
How it works:

Aggregate RNPP age columns to one total per commune (pop_by_commune).
Join population values to commune polygons via commune name (id vs COMMUNE_NOM).
Use fill = total_population to encode population with a color gradient.
Optionally add commune labels at centroids for orientation.

Join. left_join() attaches total_population to every polygon row. The join uses two different column names: polygon id (commune name) matches RNPP COMMUNE_NOM. Rows without a match keep NA for total_population (grey on the map).

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

Plot. In aes(), group = group is essential for polygons: each commune consists of many coordinate rows that must be drawn as one shape. fill = total_population maps population to colour. geom_text() uses a separate table (centroids_label); inherit.aes = FALSE prevents it from inheriting fill and group from the polygon layer. coord_quickmap() sets the map extent; scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous colour scale with readable axis labels.

ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = total_population)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: population by commune",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — sum of all age bands",
    fill = "Population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Brighter communes have higher population totals.
Luxembourg City should stand out clearly as the most populous commune.
A few communes were merged or renamed since the polygon file was built; unmatched polygons have no fill.

title: Session 4

Goal: practice map joins and pre-aggregation for cartographic input.
Tasks:

Join communes_df with pop_by_commune to map total_population by commune.

# join map polygons with RNPP commune totals
communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>

# continuous choropleth

title: Session 4 — Work with own data
text:
1.5 Example: population age pyramid data (data.public.lu)
The RNPP age pyramid by commune dataset lists population counts by commune, sex (F / M), and 5-year age bands. We use it in two steps: first a choropleth map of total population, then an Alterspyramide for one commune.

1.5.1 Load and aggregate

pyramid_url <- "https://download.data.public.lu/resources/registre-national-des-personnes-physiques-rnpp-pyramide-dage-par-commune-population-age-pyramid-per-municipality/20260407-111759/31-03-2026-rnrpp-pyramide-age-commune.csv"

age_raw <- read_csv(pyramid_url, show_col_types = FALSE)

# one row per commune: sum all age columns (both sexes)
pop_by_commune <- age_raw |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AGE"), as.numeric)) |>
  summarise(
    pop_total = sum(across(starts_with("AGE")), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = COMMUNE_NOM
  )



1.5.2 Choropleth map (total population)
Join the aggregated table to commune polygons (id = COMMUNE_NOM), then map pop_total with fill.

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

communes_rnpp <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

ggplot(communes_rnpp, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = pop_total)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.2,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: population by commune (RNPP, 31 March 2026)",
    subtitle = "Source: data.public.lu — age pyramid per municipality",
    fill = "Population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Note: a few communes were merged or renamed since the polygon file was built (e.g. Bous-Waldbredimus in the CSV vs older polygon names). Unmatched polygons appear without fill.


1.5.3 Alterspyramide for one commune
Pick a commune and reshape the wide age columns into long format. For a classic pyramid, plot men with negative counts (left) and women with positive counts (right).

commune_pick <- "Luxembourg"

age_levels <- age_raw |>
  select(starts_with("AGE")) |>
  names() |>
  str_remove("^AGE") |>
  str_replace("_", "-") |>
  (\(x) if_else(x == "100-", "100+", x))()

age_pyramid <- age_raw |>
  filter(COMMUNE_NOM == commune_pick) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("AGE"), names_to = "age_band", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    age_band = str_remove(age_band, "^AGE"),
    age_band = str_replace(age_band, "_", "-"),
    age_band = if_else(age_band == "100-", "100+", age_band),
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_levels),
    count = if_else(SEXE == "M", -count, count)
  )

ggplot(age_pyramid, aes(x = count, y = age_band, fill = SEXE)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(F = "#c0392b", M = "#2980b9"),
    labels = c(F = "Women", M = "Men")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) format(abs(x), big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Age pyramid (Alterspyramide):", commune_pick),
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — counts by 5-year age band",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Age group",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Session 4
text:
Using the same age_raw table, reshape the wide age columns into long format. For a classic pyramid, plot men with negative counts (left) and women with positive counts (right).



commune_pick <- "Differdange"

age_levels <- age_raw |>
  select(starts_with("AGE")) |>
  names() |>
  str_remove("^AGE") |>
  str_replace("_", "-") |>
  (\(x) if_else(x == "100-", "100+", x))()

Reshape. The RNPP table is wide: one column per age band. pivot_longer() stacks them into rows (age_band, count). We then clean band labels (AGE20_25 → 20-25) and fix the order with factor(..., levels = age_levels). Multiplying men’s counts by −1 places their bars on the left of the pyramid; women stay positive on the right.

age_pyramid <- age_raw |>
  filter(COMMUNE_NOM == commune_pick) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("AGE"), names_to = "age_band", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    age_band = str_remove(age_band, "^AGE"),
    age_band = str_replace(age_band, "_", "-"),
    age_band = if_else(age_band == "100-", "100+", age_band),
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_levels),
    count = if_else(SEXE == "M", -count, count)
  )

Plot. geom_col() draws horizontal bars; geom_vline(xintercept = 0) marks the centre line between women and men. scale_x_continuous(labels = ...) uses abs() so axis labels show positive numbers even though men’s values are negative.

ggplot(age_pyramid, aes(x = count, y = age_band, fill = SEXE)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(F = "#c0392b", M = "#2980b9"),
    labels = c(F = "Women", M = "Men")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) format(abs(x), big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Age pyramid:", commune_pick),
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — counts by 5-year age band",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Age group",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Change commune_pick (e.g. to "Luxembourg" or "Esch-sur-Alzette") to compare age structures.



Aggregate age_raw across all communes, keeping all age columns and grouping by sex.
Summarise. summarise(across(...), .by = SEXE) adds up every age column across all communes, but keeps women and men in separate rows. The result is still wide (one column per age band).
Age order. The pipeline on age_levels extracts column names, removes the AGE prefix, and turns underscores into hyphens. The anonymous function \(x) if_else(...) is a short way to relabel the top band 100- as 100+.
Long format. The same pivot_longer() + mutate() steps as above turn the national table into pyramid-ready data.

age_total <- age_raw |>
  summarise(
    across(starts_with("AGE"), \(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .by = SEXE
  )

age_levels <- age_total |>
  select(starts_with("AGE")) |>
  names() |>
  str_remove("^AGE") |>
  str_replace("_", "-") |>
  (\(x) if_else(x == "100-", "100+", x))()

age_pyramid <- age_total |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("AGE"), names_to = "age_band", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    age_band = str_remove(age_band, "^AGE"),
    age_band = str_replace(age_band, "_", "-"),
    age_band = if_else(age_band == "100-", "100+", age_band),
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_levels),
    count = if_else(SEXE == "M", -count, count)
  )

ggplot(age_pyramid, aes(x = count, y = age_band, fill = SEXE)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(F = "#c0392b", M = "#2980b9"),
    labels = c(F = "Women", M = "Men")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) format(abs(x), big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Age pyramid: Luxembourg"),
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — counts by 5-year age band",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Age group",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Session 4
text:
The RNPP table has separate rows for F and M. After summing population per commune and sex, we can plot two choropleths side by side with facet_wrap(~ SEXE).
How it works:

Aggregate total_population by COMMUNE_NOM and SEXE (not merged across sexes).
Join to communes_df — each commune polygon appears twice (once per sex).
Add facet_wrap(~ SEXE) so ggplot draws one map panel per sex.


pop_by_commune_sex <- age_raw |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AGE"), as.numeric)) |>
  summarise(
    total_population = sum(across(starts_with("AGE")), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(COMMUNE_NOM, SEXE)
  )

communes_pop_sex <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune_sex, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

Warning in left_join(communes_df, pop_by_commune_sex, by = c(id = "COMMUNE_NOM")): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.

ggplot(communes_pop_sex, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = total_population)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ SEXE,
    labeller = labeller(SEXE = c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Population by commune and sex",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — same fill scale in both panels",
    fill = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))









facet_wrap(~ SEXE) splits the plot into one panel per sex. The formula ~ SEXE means “create facets from the SEXE column”. Each panel reuses the same geom_polygon() call; ggplot filters the data automatically.
labeller = labeller(...) renames facet strip labels (F → “Women”, M → “Men”) without changing the underlying data.
scale_fill_viridis_c() defines one continuous colour scale for both panels, so darker/brighter communes are comparable across women and men.
theme(strip.text = ...) formats the facet titles (the strips above each small map).

Both panels share the same colour scale by default, which makes the two maps comparable.

section: 2.2 Variant statistics by age, gender, education, and dialect area
text:
2.2 Variant statistics by age, gender, education, and dialect area
Reshape the four sociolinguistic variables into long format, then compute counts and row-wise shares (distribution of variants within each age group, etc.).
Convert to character. Alter, Geschlecht, and the other columns are factors or ordered factors. pivot_longer() needs a common type in the values column, so we convert them to character first.
Long format. pivot_longer() stacks the four columns into two new ones: variable (which social factor) and level (the actual category, e.g. “25 bis 34”).
Counts and shares. count() tallies recordings per social group and variant. group_by(variable, level) + mutate(share = n / sum(n)) computes the proportion of each variant within each age band (or gender, etc.) — the values in one row of the output sum to 1.

variant_by_social <- butterfly_variants |>
  mutate(across(
    c(Alter, Geschlecht, Ausbildung, Dialektgebiet),
    \(x) as.character(x)
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(Alter, Geschlecht, Ausbildung, Dialektgebiet),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "level"
  ) |>
  count(variable, level, Variant_Päiperlek) |>
  group_by(variable, level) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(variable, level, desc(n))

Join to commune polygons and plot the dominant variant:

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")

communes_butterfly <- communes_df |>
  left_join(commune_variants, by = c("id" = "Gemeng"))

ggplot(communes_butterfly, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = dominant_variant)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3", na.value = "grey85") +
  labs(
    title = "Dominant butterfly variant by commune",
    subtitle = "Schnessen / butterfly.rds — communes without recordings in grey",
    fill = "Dominant variant"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
